Yesterday saw two conflicting reports about next year's iPhone 20th anniversary version, which is said to embody Apple's long-term vision of "a single slab of glass."

We already had somewhat conflicting reports about what to expect, but yesterday's divergence is the biggest yet...

Here's what's known so far

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive has frequently talked about his long-term vision that the iPhone will eventually evolve into "a single slab of glass." The company is widely believed to still be holding onto that vision even after Ive's departure.

Although Apple generally doesn't make a big deal of celebrating various anniversaries of its products, the prevailing market view is that they're targeting achieving this vision by the iPhone's 20th anniversary if at all possible. This version would likely embed Face ID technology under the display, and there's also a chance the front-facing camera would be similarly hidden beneath the display.

However, we've already seen conflicting reports about what to expect. While it was initially thought to be a standalone model similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, more recent reports indicate this design will instead be applied to next year's iPhone Pro models.

Sequentially that would be the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple may also want to use the anniversary occasion to skip that number and go straight to the iPhone 20 naming.

Yesterday's conflicting reports

Yesterday things got even more muddled, with an analyst claiming Apple had abandoned the idea of launching an all-glass iPhone next year.

However, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman quickly pushed back on that claim.

What seems more likely

The key point here is that Apple's vision for the iPhone doesn't have a single finish line. Whatever Apple plans to release next year will simply be one more step — or several steps — closer to that sci-fi vision of "a single slab of glass."

The question isn't whether that goal will be achieved next year, but how far Apple will get toward that vision. But whether it's one step or several, this certainly won't be the final step in iPhone design evolution.

In fact, Gurman revealed that Apple has retreated somewhat from where it had originally hoped to be by next year.

It's quite possible the Jefferies analyst heard the same news, but only heard it more recently and thus interpreted it as a complete abandonment of the plan.

My own expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap forward — comparable to the milestone when the iPhone X launched — but with even more to come in subsequent years. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will have enough breakthroughs for Apple to attach some sort of special branding to it: whether it's labeled as the 20th anniversary iPhone (which I think is unlikely), given another special name, or skipping a generation to go straight to iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
